summary: This standards-track memo registers the text/red MIME sub-type. Red stands for redundant. The actual RTP packetisation for the type is given in RFC 2198.

plainLanguage.summary: When text is sent over a real-time connection, a lost packet loses the words. This RFC registers a media type called text/red, where red stands for redundant, so that a sender can send a low-bandwidth copy alongside the real text and the receiver can rebuild a lost packet. It also explains how to write that media type into a session description.

questions: what is redundant text in rtp
what is the text red mime type
how does text/red map to sdp
what are the rate and pt parameters in text/red
subtitle: The MIME type for sending redundant copies of text, so a lost packet does not lose the words.

tldr.problem: Text sent over a real-time transport can be lost like any other packet, and the RFC for redundant audio does not itself tell applications how to label redundant text.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the MIME sub-type text/red, whose name stands for redundant, with a rate parameter for the clock rate and a pt parameter listing the primary and secondary payload types, and it shows how those fields map into a Session Description Protocol session description.
tldr.outcome: Text streaming and conferencing tools gained a registered media type that says a stream carries redundant copies, with the packetisation itself left to RFC 2198.

facts.label: Usage restriction
facts.value: Transfer via RTP only, not a storage format

today: RFC 4102 is a Proposed Standard that registers the text/red media type and has not been obsoleted, so the registration and its SDP mapping still describe how a redundant text stream is labelled. It was later extended for a related purpose by RFC 6354, which adds support for forward-shifted RTP redundancy.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Text is an important component of any multimedia communication system. Like audio, the transport of text can benefit from the use of redundancy in order to improve reliability and the end-user experience.

RFC 2198 defines an RTP payload format for redundant audio data, and the format defined there is quite suitable for providing redundancy for text as well as audio. RFC 4103 specifies one usage of RFC 2198 and the text/red MIME type for the transport of redundant text data.

This memo provides the MIME sub-type registration information for text/red. While it focuses on the use of this MIME sub-type in the Session Description Protocol, the application of the sub-type is not restricted to SDP. The abstract is explicit that red is short for redundant and that the actual RTP packetisation for this MIME type is specified in RFC 2198, so this document adds the naming, not the format.
sections.plainLanguage: Redundant text means sending a smaller copy of the text alongside the real thing, so a lost packet can be rebuilt. The format for that was already defined for audio; this RFC only adds the media type name for text.

sections.title: The text/red Registration
sections.content:
One new MIME sub-type has been registered by IANA. The MIME media type name is text and the MIME subtype name is RED. The registration also records that interoperability considerations are none, that the published specification is RFC 2198, that the applications which use this media type are text streaming and conferencing tools, and that the intended usage is COMMON. The change controller is the AVT Working Group, delegated from the IESG.

Two restrictions govern how the type may be used. It is defined only for transfer via RTP, and it shall not be defined for a storage format. The encoding considerations section is included only because of the requirements in RFC 3555, and points back to those restrictions on usage.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration says the type is called text/red, that it is meant for live streaming over RTP, and that it is not a file format. RFC 2198 remains the document that says how the packets are built.

sections.title: Required and Optional Parameters
sections.content:
The registration defines two required parameters. The first is rate, the RTP clock rate of the payload carried within the RTP packet. Typically this rate is 1000, but other rates may be specified, and it must be set equal to the clock rate of the text payload format carried as the primary encoding.

The second required parameter is pt, a comma-separated ordered list of RTP payload types enumerating the primary, secondary and further encodings in accordance with RFC 2198. Because a comma is a special character, the list must be a quoted string. For static payload types each list element is simply the type number. For dynamic payload types each list element maps the dynamic payload type number to an embedded MIME content-type specification for the payload format, using the format dynamic-payload-type "=" content-type.

If the content-type string includes a comma it must be a quoted string, and it may be quoted even when it does not include a comma. Because the content-type string is part of a list that must itself be a quoted string, the quotation marks must be quoted with backslash quoting as specified in RFC 2045, and that requirement is applied recursively if the content-type string itself contains a quoted string.

The optional parameters are ptime and maxptime, which are originally defined in RFC 2327 and RFC 3267 respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: Two parameters must always be given. The rate says how fast the text is clocked, usually 1000. The pt parameter lists, in order, the payload type of the main encoding and then the payload types of the redundant copies.

sections.title: Mapping to SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The information carried in the MIME media type specification has a specific mapping to fields in the Session Description Protocol, which is commonly used to describe RTP sessions. When SDP is used to specify a session employing the RFC 2198 format in a text session, the mapping is as follows. The MIME type, text, goes in the SDP m= line as the media name. The value of the parameter rate goes in a=rtpmap. The MIME subtype, RED, goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name. The parameters ptime and maxptime go in the a=ptime and a=maxptime attributes respectively.

The pt parameter is mapped to an a=fmtp attribute by eliminating the parameter name and changing the commas to slashes. For example, pt="101,102" maps to a=fmtp:99 101/102, where 99 is the payload type of the redundancy frames. The single quote marks used in that example are not present in the actual message encoding, but are present in the document only for readability. The level of redundancy is shown by the number of elements in the payload type list.

Any dynamic payload type in the list must be represented by its payload type number and not by its content-type. The mapping of payload types to the content-type is done using the normal SDP procedures with a=rtpmap. For each redundancy payload type defined, the ordering of the primary and redundancy encodings is fixed; if more than one combination of primary and redundancy encodings is desired, multiple redundancy payload types need to be defined.
sections.plainLanguage: A session description says what media a stream carries. This section maps each part of the media type onto the right line of that description, and shows that the list of payload types becomes a slash-separated list in the format line.

sections.title: An Example Session Description
sections.content:
The RFC gives a complete example of an SDP session that carries a redundant text stream. The media line announces a text session on port 11000 using RTP with two payload types. The first a=rtpmap line gives payload type 98 as the t140 text encoding at 1000 Hz. The second gives payload type 100 as the red encoding at 1000 Hz, and the a=fmtp line states that the redundancy stream uses payload type 98 as its own copy.

Read together, the example describes a session whose primary text is sent in payload type 98 and whose redundant copy is carried in payload type 100.
sections.plainLanguage: This short session description shows the whole mechanism: one payload type carries the text, another carries the redundant copy of it, and the format line says which one to copy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations listed in RFC 2198 apply. The RFC adds that text data, perhaps even more so than audio data, is susceptible to unwanted modification that may lead to undesired results. To prevent modification of the primary, secondary or header information, payload integrity protection over at least the complete RTP packet is recommended, for example using SRTP as specified in RFC 3711.
sections.plainLanguage: Text can be altered in ways that cause real harm, so the RFC recommends protecting the whole packet, for example with SRTP. The rest of the security guidance comes from the redundant audio document it builds on.

viz.caption: THE PARAMETERS OF THE text/red MEDIA TYPE

items.title: rate (required)
items.text: The RTP clock rate of the payload. Typically 1000, and it must equal the clock rate of the primary text encoding.

items.title: pt (required)
items.text: A quoted, comma-separated ordered list of payload types: the primary encoding first, then the redundant ones.

items.title: ptime (optional)
items.text: The time each packet is generated, originally defined in RFC 2327.

items.title: maxptime (optional)
items.text: The longest gap between packets, originally defined in RFC 3267.

viz.caption: WHERE EACH MEDIA TYPE FIELD GOES IN A SESSION DESCRIPTION

cells: a=fmtp, with the commas changed to slashes

viz.caption: THE EXAMPLE SESSION DESCRIPTION FROM RFC 4102 SECTION 4

data.title: Example SDP
data.code:
m=text 11000 RTP/AVP 98 100
a=rtpmap:98 t140/1000
a=rtpmap:100 red/1000
a=fmtp:100 98/98
